title: Treatment planning, referral & follow-up
blurb: How treatment is planned, when and where patients are referred, urgent suspected cancer referrals, writing and tracking referral letters, and arranging follow-up.
question: At a check-up the dentist finds an ulcer on the side of a patient's tongue that the patient says has been there for about a month. The dentist asks you to prepare an urgent referral. What must the letter include, how should it be sent, and what do you do after it has gone?

teach.body: After assessment the dentist makes a diagnosis and discusses the options with the patient, including risks, benefits and costs, so the patient can give valid consent. The agreed plan is written down; in NHS England a treatment plan form (FP17DC) is given for Band 2 and 3 courses. Dental nurses don't diagnose or plan treatment, but you record accurately, support communication and book appointments as the dentist prescribes. When care is beyond the practice, the dentist refers.

steps.label: Written plan
steps.sub: Recorded and given to the patient

steps.label: Treat or refer
steps.sub: In practice, or onward to another service

children.label: Other services
children.sub: GP, community dental, stop smoking, safeguarding

teach.caption: NHS England grades complexity in levels: Level 1 is general practice, Levels 2 and 3 need enhanced or specialist skills. Primary care is general and community dentistry; secondary care is hospital and specialist services.

teach.h: A lesion that needs urgent referral
teach.caption: An ulcerated, red and white raised lesion on the side of the tongue. A lesion like this that hasn't healed in 3 weeks needs an urgent suspected cancer referral.

teach.body: NICE guidance (NG12) says a suspected cancer referral, for an appointment within 2 weeks, should be considered for unexplained ulceration in the mouth lasting more than 3 weeks or a persistent unexplained lump in the neck. Dentists also refer urgently for a lump on the lip or in the mouth, or a red or red-and-white patch, consistent with oral cancer. It is still widely called the '2-week wait'. Use the local urgent pathway, the same day, and make sure the patient understands it is important to attend.

teach.h: How fast? Matching urgency to route

items: Patient details: full name, date of birth, address, phone numbers and NHS number if known.
Referrer's details, the patient's GP, and the date of referral.
The reason for referral and how urgent it is, in clear words.
History and findings: complaint, how long, examination results, investigations done.
Medical history, medicines, allergies and relevant social history such as smoking and alcohol.
Images or radiographs enclosed, the patient's agreement to the referral, and any needs such as an interpreter or wheelchair access.

teach.h: Your role once the dentist decides to refer
teach.body: Prepare the letter as instructed and check every detail. Send it securely by the approved electronic system or secure NHS email, never by ordinary email. Log it in the referral tracker, record it in the notes, and copy the GP if required. Chase it if no acknowledgement arrives and tell the dentist if the patient hasn't been seen. Explain to the patient what happens next, within your role. As part of the wider health team you can also signpost, for example to stop smoking services.

items.label: an unexplained mouth ulcer lasting longer needs urgent referral
NICE recall range for adults, set by risk

teach.text: Don't mix up the two numbers. Three weeks is how long an unexplained ulcer has lasted before it triggers an urgent referral. Two weeks is how quickly the patient should be seen once referred. And never reassure a patient that 'it's probably nothing': explain the dentist wants a specialist to check it quickly.

items: Dentists diagnose and plan; nurses record, communicate, book and track.
Refer to specialists, hospital services or wider health services as needed.
Ulcer over 3 weeks or unexplained neck lump: urgent suspected cancer referral (seen within 2 weeks).
Letters: patient details, reason and urgency, history, medical history, images; sent securely.
Log, chase and record every referral, and book follow-up as prescribed.

summary: You can now describe how treatment is planned and consented, choose the right referral route and urgency, recognise when an urgent suspected cancer referral is needed, write and send a complete referral securely, and track it and arrange follow-up.

A.q: A patient has had an unexplained ulcer on the floor of the mouth for over three weeks. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Review it again at the next routine recall
Refer the patient to the practice hygienist today
Advise an antiseptic mouthwash for a month
Urgent suspected cancer referral by the dentist
A.why: An unexplained ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks meets NICE criteria for an urgent suspected cancer referral.

whyNot.0: Waiting until the next recall could delay the diagnosis of a cancer.
whyNot.1: Hygienists don't diagnose suspected cancers; it needs a specialist assessment.
whyNot.2: A mouthwash doesn't investigate the cause and delays referral.

A.q: Who is responsible for diagnosing the patient's condition and planning their treatment?
options: The dental nurse
The receptionist
The dentist
The practice manager
A.why: Diagnosis and treatment planning are the dentist's role. The GDC states dental nurses do not diagnose or plan treatment.

whyNot.0: Dental nurses support and record but do not diagnose or plan treatment.
whyNot.1: Receptionists manage bookings and records, not clinical decisions.
whyNot.3: The practice manager runs the business side, not clinical care.

A.q: How should a referral letter containing patient information be sent?
options: By the approved secure referral system
By any email account that is quickest
By text message to the specialist's phone
Through the post with no record kept
A.why: Referrals contain confidential health information, so they go through approved secure systems and are logged.

whyNot.1: Ordinary email isn't secure enough for patient health information.
whyNot.2: Texting a personal phone breaches confidentiality and leaves no proper record.
whyNot.3: Any method must be recorded so the referral can be tracked.

B.q: Which of these must be included in a referral letter?
options: The practice's opening hours
The patient's account balance
The reason for referral and its urgency
The nurse's personal mobile phone number
B.why: The receiving clinician needs to know why the patient is being referred and how quickly they need to be seen.

whyNot.0: Opening hours aren't clinical information the specialist needs.
whyNot.1: Financial details aren't relevant to the referral.
whyNot.3: Personal staff details should never be included.

B.q: Three weeks after an urgent referral was sent, the patient rings to say they have heard nothing. What should you do?
options: Tell them to wait, as hospitals are very busy
Re-send it without telling the dentist
Ask them to book a routine check-up
Chase the referral and inform the dentist
B.why: Urgent referrals must be tracked. If the patient hasn't heard, chase it with the receiving service and let the dentist know.

whyNot.0: An urgent referral should have led to an appointment by now; waiting risks harm.
whyNot.1: The dentist is responsible for the referral and must know it may have gone astray.
whyNot.2: A routine check-up doesn't solve the missing urgent appointment.

B.q: A patient's teeth are complex to extract and need a specialist oral surgeon. In NHS England complexity terms, this is most likely:
options: Level 1 care in general practice
Level 2 or 3 care with enhanced skills
Routine recall in general dental practice
Emergency care in A&E
B.why: NHS England grades complexity: Level 1 is general practice, while Levels 2 and 3 need enhanced or specialist skills.

whyNot.0: Level 1 covers care a general dentist provides routinely.
whyNot.2: A recall is a check-up, not management of complex surgery.
whyNot.3: A planned complex extraction isn't an emergency.

C.q: Under NICE guidance, how quickly should a patient referred on an urgent suspected cancer pathway be offered an appointment?
options: Within 3 weeks
Within 2 weeks
Within 6 weeks
Within 18 weeks
C.why: NICE describes the suspected cancer pathway referral as being for an appointment within 2 weeks.

whyNot.0: Three weeks is how long an ulcer has lasted before referral, not the appointment target.
whyNot.2: Six weeks is too long for a suspected cancer.
whyNot.3: Eighteen weeks relates to routine elective treatment, not urgent cancer referrals.

C.q: NICE recommends recall intervals between oral health reviews for adults of:
options: 3 to 24 months
1 to 6 months
6 months for everyone
12 to 36 months
C.why: NICE CG19 sets adult recall intervals from 3 to 24 months depending on the patient's risk.

whyNot.1: This range is too short and isn't the NICE recommendation.
whyNot.2: NICE moved away from a fixed six-month recall for everyone.
whyNot.3: The maximum for adults is 24 months, not 36.

C.q: A patient being referred urgently asks the nurse, 'Is it cancer?' What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell them it is almost certainly nothing to worry about
Confirm that it looks very much like cancer to you
Explain the dentist wants a specialist to check it soon
Say you can't discuss it and change the subject
C.why: Nurses don't diagnose. Be honest that a specialist needs to check it quickly and make sure the dentist explains the reason.

whyNot.0: False reassurance could stop the patient attending an important appointment.
whyNot.1: Diagnosing is outside the dental nurse's scope of practice.
whyNot.3: Avoiding the question is unkind and may leave the patient confused about the urgency.

reteach.title: A referral is a relay baton
reteach.question: In a relay race the baton has to be passed cleanly, and someone has to check it reached the next runner. How is a referral like that?

blocks.body: The dentist decides the patient needs another runner: a specialist, hospital or other service. The referral letter is the baton. It has to carry everything the next person needs (who the patient is, why, how urgent, history, images) and be handed over securely. A dropped baton is a lost referral, so the team logs it, checks it has been received and chases it if not. Meanwhile the patient needs to know what happens next.

blocks.text: An ulcer that has lasted 3 weeks doesn't wait for the next recall. Urgent means today.

explain.body: The dentist diagnoses, explains options, risks, benefits and costs, and records the agreed plan. In NHS England the patient gets an FP17DC treatment plan for Band 2 and 3 courses. Nurses record, communicate and book.

test.q: What must the patient understand before agreeing to a treatment plan?
options: The options, risks, benefits and costs
Only the date of the first appointment
The dental nurse's qualifications
How the laboratory makes crowns
test.why: Valid consent needs the patient to understand their options, including risks, benefits and costs.

whyNot.1: Appointment dates don't make consent valid.
whyNot.2: Staff qualifications aren't part of consent to treatment.
whyNot.3: Laboratory methods aren't needed for valid consent.

explain.body: Specialist practices handle orthodontics, oral surgery, periodontics and endodontics. Hospital services take complex and suspected cancer cases. GPs, community dental services, stop smoking services and safeguarding teams are part of the wider pathway.

test.q: A patient wants help to stop smoking. Where can the dental team signpost them?
options: The dental laboratory
An oral surgeon
A local stop smoking service
An orthodontist
test.why: The dental team is an access point to wider healthcare and can signpost to local stop smoking services.

whyNot.0: Laboratories make appliances and have no patient-support role.
whyNot.1: Oral surgeons treat surgical problems, not smoking cessation.

explain.body: An unexplained mouth ulcer over 3 weeks, a persistent neck lump, a lump on the lip or in the mouth, or a red or red-and-white patch: urgent referral on the local pathway, for an appointment within 2 weeks.

test.q: Which finding should trigger an urgent suspected cancer referral?
options: A broken filling with sharp edges
A painful ulcer that healed on its own in a week
Bleeding gums when brushing
A red and white patch with no clear cause
test.why: A red or red-and-white patch consistent with oral cancer is a reason for urgent referral.

whyNot.0: A broken filling needs repair, not cancer referral.
whyNot.1: An ulcer that heals within a week is unlikely to be cancer.

explain.body: Include patient details, reason and urgency, history and findings, medical history, images and any special needs. Send securely, log it, record it, chase it and book follow-up as prescribed.

test.q: Why is every referral entered in a referral log or tracker?
options: So the patient can be charged a fee
So it can be followed up if it goes missing
So the GDC can inspect it each month
So the nurse can sign it off as complete
test.why: A log lets the team check each referral was received and acted on, so no patient falls through the gaps.

whyNot.0: The log is a safety tool, not a billing record.
whyNot.2: The GDC doesn't inspect referral logs monthly.
whyNot.3: The dentist remains responsible; the log is for tracking, not sign-off.
